examples.en: Applications open tomorrow morning.

examples.ko: 드디어 두 나라 사이의 회담이 개시됐어요.
examples.en: Talks between the two countries have finally begun.

examples.ko: 공사가 개시되는 날부터 길이 막힐 거예요.
examples.en: From the day construction begins, the road will be blocked.
I'll let you know by text when registration opens.
The tickets sold out as soon as sales began.

examples.ko: 조사가 개시된 지 한 달이 지났어요.
examples.en: A month has passed since the investigation began.

explain: 공식적인 일, 절차, 행사, 판매가 시작될 때 써요. 일상 대화에서 '수업이 시작돼요'는 '개시돼요'보다 훨씬 자연스러워요. 글, 공지, 뉴스에서 더 많이 보여요.
explain_en: Used when an official matter, procedure, event or sale begins. In daily talk, 시작돼요 sounds much more natural than 개시돼요 for something like a class. You will see it more in written notices and news.

examples.en: The day applications open is next Monday.
Do you know when this service starts?

examples.ko: 영업 개시일을 한 달 뒤로 미뤘어요.
examples.en: We pushed the business start date back by a month.

examples.ko: 공사 개시일에 맞춰 짐을 모두 옮겨 주세요.
examples.en: Please move all your belongings out in time for the construction start date.

examples.ko: 접수 개시일 아침부터 사람들이 줄을 섰어요.
examples.en: People lined up from the morning of the day registration opened.

examples.ko: 판매 개시일이 되자마자 표가 다 팔렸어요.
examples.en: The tickets sold out as soon as sales opened.

explain: 신청, 판매, 공사, 영업 같은 말 뒤에 붙어서 공지나 뉴스에서 많이 나와요. 반대로 끝나는 날은 '종료일'이나 '마감일'이라고 해요. 평소 대화에서는 그냥 '시작하는 날'이라고도 말해요.
explain_en: It attaches to words like application, sales, construction and business, and appears often in notices and news. The opposite is '종료일' or '마감일'. In casual talk people also just say '시작하는 날'.

examples.en: If today is Monday, four days from now is Friday.
I'm going to see a movie with a friend four days from today.
The move has been set for the morning four days from now.
I have to finish this report by four days from now.
I think the rain will stop around four days from now.
The plan for four days from now isn't confirmed yet.

explain: 오늘부터 순서대로 '내일, 모레, 글피, 그글피'예요. 사흘 뒤가 글피, 나흘 뒤가 그글피예요. 일상에서는 '나흘 뒤'나 '4일 뒤'처럼 말하기도 해요.
explain_en: Counting from today the order is '내일, 모레, 글피, 그글피'. Three days from now is 글피 and four days from now is 그글피. In daily talk people also say '나흘 뒤' or '4일 뒤'.

en: around the end of the month

examples.en: I'm going to move around the end of this month.
I'll come visit you sometime around the end of the month.
My pay usually comes in around the end of the month.
It often snows around the end of December.
It's around the end of the month, so there's no moon in the night sky.

examples.ko: 그믐께에 맞춰 책을 다 읽으려고 해요.
examples.en: I'm trying to finish the book by around the end of the month.

explain: '그믐'에 '-께'가 붙어서 그믐 무렵을 말해요. 일상에서는 '월말쯤'이라고도 하고, 반대로 달의 중간쯤은 '보름께'라고 해요.
explain_en: '-께' is added to '그믐' to mean around the end of the month. In daily talk people also say '월말쯤', and the middle of the month is '보름께'.

examples.en: In the off-season, the villagers go on trips.

examples.ko: 저희 집은 요즘이 농한기라서 조금 한가해요.
examples.en: It's the off-season for farming at our house, so we're a bit free.
When the off-season comes, the country village gets quiet.
We decided to repair the house during the off-season.
Even in the off-season, greenhouse farming is busy.
The off-season usually comes in winter.

explain: 반대말은 농사일이 가장 바쁜 때를 가리키는 '농번기'예요. 가게나 일이 한가한 철은 '비수기'라고 하고, 농한기는 농사 이야기에서 써요.
explain_en: Its opposite is '농번기', the busiest farming season. For slow seasons in shops or other jobs people say '비수기', while 농한기 is used when talking about farming.

en: absence of holidays; absence of rest

examples.ko: 이 약국은 연중무휴라서 명절에도 문을 열어요.
examples.en: This pharmacy never closes, so it's open even on holidays.

examples.ko: 연중무휴라고 쓰여 있어서 일요일에 갔는데 문이 닫혀 있었어요.
examples.en: It said open all year round, so I went on Sunday, but it was closed.
The convenience store in my neighborhood operates every day of the year.

examples.ko: 연중무휴 식당이라서 언제든 갈 수 있어요.
examples.en: It's a restaurant that never closes, so you can go anytime.
It's reassuring that there's a hospital nearby open every day.

examples.ko: 연중무휴라는 말만 믿지 말고 전화해 보세요.
examples.en: Don't just trust the 'open every day' sign; try calling.

explain: 거의 항상 '연중무휴'로 가게 앞이나 광고에서 만나요. 반대로 쉬는 날은 '휴무'나 '정기 휴무'라고 해요. 그래도 명절이나 특별한 날에는 쉬기도 하니 가기 전에 확인하면 좋아요.
explain_en: You almost always meet it as '연중무휴' (open all year) on shop signs and ads. The opposite idea is '휴무' or '정기 휴무' (regular closing day). Even so, some places still close on holidays or special days, so it's good to check before you go.

examples.en: The meeting date is still not confirmed.

examples.ko: 일정이 미확정이라 비행기 표를 못 샀어요.
examples.en: The schedule isn't confirmed, so I couldn't buy a plane ticket.

examples.ko: 미확정 소식은 말하지 않는 게 좋아요.
examples.en: It's better not to share unconfirmed news.

examples.ko: 출연자가 미확정 상태라서 방송 준비가 늦어요.
examples.en: The cast isn't finalized, so broadcast preparation is delayed.
If the place isn't settled, it's hard to book in advance.
It was reported that the pass result is still undecided.

explain: 반의어는 '확정'이에요. 일정이나 결과처럼 아직 정해지지 않은 것에 쓰고, 비슷한 말로 '미정'이 있어요. '미확정 상태', '미확정이다'로 많이 써요.
explain_en: The opposite is '확정'. It is used for things like schedules and results that aren't settled yet, and '미정' is a similar word. It commonly appears as '미확정 상태' and '미확정이다'.

examples.en: It will take about an hour to get to the airport.

examples.ko: 소요된 비용은 나중에 돌려받을 수 있어요.
examples.en: You can get back the money spent later.

examples.ko: 비자를 받는 데 보통 2주가 소요되는 편이에요.
examples.en: Getting a visa usually takes around two weeks.
The costs are running higher than expected.

examples.ko: 서류 심사에 시간이 소요돼서 많이 늦어졌어요.
examples.en: The document review took time, so it got delayed a lot.
How long does it take by taxi?

explain: '시간이 걸리다'와 같은 상황에서 쓰는 격식 있는 말이에요. 공지나 안내문에서 '소요 시간', '소요 비용'처럼 자주 보여요. 친구와 말할 때는 '걸려요'가 훨씬 자연스러워요.
explain_en: A formal counterpart of 시간이 걸리다. Signs and notices often show 소요 시간 (time needed) and 소요 비용 (cost needed). With friends, 걸려요 sounds much more natural.

examples.en: Our school's autumn sports day is an annual event.

examples.ko: 이 축제는 해마다 열리는 연례행사가 됐어요.
examples.en: This festival has become an annual event held every year.
I'm going to the countryside for the yearly kimchi-making.
It's an annual event, so I cleared my schedule in advance.
I'd feel sorry if I missed the annual event.
Like a yearly ritual, we argue about the same thing every year.

explain: 해마다 때가 정해져 열리는 행사를 말해요. 매년 되풀이되는 일을 농담처럼 말할 때도 '또 연례행사네'라고 해요. 같은 말로 '해마다 하는 행사'라고 풀어서 말하기도 해요.
explain_en: It refers to an event held at a fixed time every year. People also joke about things that repeat every year by saying '또 연례행사네'. You can also spell it out as '해마다 하는 행사'.

examples.ko: 저희는 다음 주에 여행을 예정하고 있어요.
examples.en: We are planning a trip next week.
I scheduled the meeting for Friday.
I will set the show for three p.m.
They're a couple planning to marry next year.
I planned my vacation for August, so I bought a plane ticket.

examples.ko: 예정한 날짜를 바꿔야 할 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think we have to change the planned date.

explain: 말할 때는 '계획하다'나 '~할 예정이에요'를 더 자주 써요. '예정하다'는 날짜와 시간이 정해진 일에 어울려서 공지, 뉴스에서 보여요. 막연한 생각에는 '생각 중이에요'를 써요.
explain_en: In speech, '계획하다' and '~할 예정이에요' are used more. 예정하다 suits events with a set date or time and shows up in notices and news. For a vague idea, say '생각 중이에요' (I'm thinking about it).

dis.h: fix something for a set time

p.n: 예정하다 sets a date or time for something; 계획하다 does not take a date like this naturally.

en: be finalized; be confirmed; be settled

examples.en: The schedule has not been finalized yet.
Our team's departure date has been confirmed.
I will tell you as soon as your acceptance is confirmed.
Please tell people only the finalized plan.
The day the exam results are finalized is Friday.

examples.ko: 가격이 확정돼서 포스터를 만들 수 있어요.
examples.en: The price is settled, so we can make the poster.

explain: '정해지다'는 일상에서 아무 때나 쓰지만, '확정되다'는 바뀔 수 있던 일이 마지막으로 정해졌을 때 써요. 일정·가격·합격 같은 말과 잘 어울려요. 아직 안 정해졌을 때는 '미정'이라고 해요.
explain_en: '정해지다' is the everyday word, while '확정되다' is for something that could still change and has now been settled for good. It pairs well with schedules, prices, and acceptances. When something is not yet decided, people say '미정'.

dis.h: made final and confirmed, no more changes

p.n: 결정 only says it was decided; it doesn't stress that it is now final.
